title: As Workers Shrink by 400,000, Elderly Grow by 600,000 - Seoul Economic Daily

As Workers Shrink by 400,000, Elderly Grow by 600,000 - Seoul Economic Daily

# As Workers Shrink by 400,000, Elderly Grow by 600,000

Korea Enters Super-Aged Society in Just 7 Years Five Years Faster Than Japan; Elderly Top 10 Million Working-Age Population Share Falls Below 70% for First Time Now Three People Support One Elderly Person

Published 2026.07.29. 06:41:55

By Lee Jung-hoon

Elderly visitors at Tapgol Park in Jongno-gu, Seoul, on the 28th. News1

South Korea has become a super-aged society just seven years after entering an aged society. One in five people is now 65 or older. This pace is five years faster than Japan. As the number of workers declines and the number of elderly who require pension, medical, and long-term care spending rises, the foundations of growth, public finances, and regional economies are shaking simultaneously.

According to the "2025 Population and Housing Census Results" released by Statistics Korea on the 28th, the elderly population aged 65 and older stood at 10.723 million as of November 1 last year, an increase of 601,000 (5.9%) from the previous year. The share of the elderly in the total population rose from 19.5% to 20.7%.

Generally, a society is classified as an aged society when the share of the population aged 65 and older exceeds 14%, and a super-aged society when it exceeds 20%. Korea entered an aged society in 2018, then crossed the threshold into a super-aged society seven years later.

Japan took 12 years to move from an aged society to a super-aged society. Italy took 20 years, and Germany 36 years. Korea is aging nearly twice as fast as Japan. This is why the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) rates Korea as the fastest-aging country among its member states.

Workers Fell by 1.42 Million, Elderly Rose by 2.44 Million

While the elderly population has surged, the working-age population that supports the economy is shrinking rapidly. Last year, the working-age population aged 15 to 64 stood at 35.87 million, down 393,000 (1.1%) from a year earlier. Its share of the total population also fell from 70.0% to 69.2%. It is the first time the working-age population share has dropped below 70% since annual tallies using administrative data began in 2015.

The long-term trend is even clearer. The working-age population fell by 1.418 million over five years, from 37.288 million in 2020 to 35.87 million last year. In contrast, the population aged 65 and older rose by 2.436 million over the same period, from 8.287 million to 10.723 million. The number of workers fell by nearly 1.42 million, while the number of elderly to be supported rose by about 2.44 million.

Three People Support One Elderly Person…Heavier Burden

The support burden has also grown steeply. The old-age dependency ratio, which represents the number of elderly that 100 working-age people must support, jumped from 27.9 in 2024 to 29.9 last year. Now about three working-age people must support one elderly person.

The problem is that this change is not simply a matter of population numbers. When the number of workers declines, labor input decreases, lowering the potential growth rate. The population paying taxes and social insurance premiums also shrinks. In contrast, fiscal spending targeting the elderly, such as pensions and medical and long-term care, is rising rapidly.

This is why there are concerns that the country could fall into a vicious cycle in which low growth reduces fiscal capacity, and increased welfare spending in turn drags down growth.

Growth in the 0% Range in the 2040s…Negative Growth if Reform Is Delayed

The Korea Development Institute (KDI) forecast that, due to the decline in the working-age population, labor input's contribution to growth will turn negative around 2030. It analyzed that if total factor productivity continues the trend of the past decade, the potential growth rate will fall to the low 1% range in 2030 and drop to around 0% in the 2040s.

It also warned that if structural reform is delayed, the point of entering negative growth could be moved up to the early 2040s. This means that even as the population declines, if productivity cannot be raised, the Korean economy could effectively stop growing from a little over a decade from now.

Fiscal pressure is also expected to intensify. The OECD projected that Korea's fiscal spending on health, long-term care, and pensions will rise to 17.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2060. This is because the number of people paying premiums and taxes is declining while the number of people using pension, medical, and long-term care services is surging.

Even if the birth rate rebounds, it cannot resolve the immediate labor shortage. It takes more than 20 years for a child born now to enter the labor market. Ultimately, the shrinking labor force must be supplemented through productivity gains, continued employment of the elderly, and expanded foreign labor.

Raise Productivity With AI, and Elderly Must Work Longer in Primary Jobs

First, there are calls to spread artificial intelligence (AI) and robots not only in manufacturing but throughout the service industry, including distribution, lodging, food, and care. Education and vocational training must also be strengthened to raise the value added produced by each worker. KDI analyzed that if the growth rate of total factor productivity is raised through the spread of AI and reform of the economic structure, slight growth could be maintained even in 2050.

The labor market structure, in which the elderly are forced into early retirement from their primary jobs and then brought back into low-wage jobs, must also be changed.

Korea's employment rate for those aged 65 to 69 was 57% in 2024, more than double the OECD average of 26%. On the surface, it appears the elderly are working actively, but many move to jobs with low wages and job stability after retiring from their primary jobs. The elderly employment rate is high, but job quality is low.

Experts point out that it is difficult to solve the problem by uniformly extending the retirement age alone. If the employment period is only extended while the seniority-based wage system remains in place, companies' labor cost burden will increase and youth hiring could shrink.

They argue that the wage system should be changed to focus on jobs and performance, and combined with retraining and job-transition support, so that elderly workers can work longer in their primary jobs while making use of their skills.

Suk Jae-eun, a professor of social welfare at Hallym University, said, "We must hurry to reorganize the social system to fit a super-aged society," adding, "To reduce the burden from the growing elderly population, we must revitalize the elderly labor market and change not only pensions but also the medical use and coverage systems."

Foreigners Rose, but Filled Only 11% of Native Decline

The influx of foreigners is partially cushioning the labor force decline, but it is insufficient to replace the decline in the native population. Last year, foreigners aged 15 to 64 numbered 1.883 million, up 50,000 from the previous year. Over the same period, the native working-age population, excluding foreigners, fell by 443,000. The increase in foreigners filled only about 11% of the decline in the native population.

However, in farming and fishing villages and manufacturing-dense areas, foreigners have already established themselves as a core workforce supporting regional economies. Last year, of the nation's 229 cities, counties, and districts, 12 had foreigners making up more than 10% of the total population.

In Yeongam-gun, South Jeolla Province, 19.8% of residents were foreigners, or one in five. In Eumseong-gun, North Chungcheong Province, the figure reached 17.7%, and in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, 13.4%. The number of areas where production sites in farming and fishing villages and industrial complexes could grind to a halt if foreigners were to leave is increasing.

There are also concerns that a shortage of workers at industrial sites and the problem of regional extinction cannot be solved together with an approach that supplies foreign labor only in the short term as needed. They argue that housing, education, medical care, Korean-language education, and family-accompaniment policies must be organized so that foreign workers can settle in local communities.

Cho Young-tae, a professor at Seoul National University's Graduate School of Public Health, said, "This kind of change in the population structure was already predicted," adding, "We must prepare for the future by considering not only the number of the population but also its qualitative characteristics and changes in the industrial structure."

Original reporting by Lee Jung-hoon for Seoul Economic Daily.
